item.title: Ollama Tool Calls: Object vs String Arguments on Two API Surfaces
item.description: Same prompt, same qwen3:0.6b call: /api/chat returns arguments as an object, /v1/chat/completions as a JSON string, and replaying either history returns HTTP 400. The two error strings, a tested normaliser, and the streaming shape that looks hung.
item.content:encoded:
A coding agent works for an afternoon against Ollama’s native /api/chat. Then someone points the OpenAI SDK at http://localhost:11434/v1 to reuse an existing client, or a library switches endpoints underneath the agent. The first turn still works. The second turn is where the run dies, in one of two ways that look unrelated:

  • the executor calls args["path"] and gets TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str', because the arguments arrived as a JSON string;
  • or the client stores the native assistant message, sends it back to /v1/chat/completions, and gets HTTP 400 before a single token is generated.

Both failures have the same cause: the two surfaces of the same server encode a tool call in incompatible ways. On Ollama 0.20.3, non-streaming, with qwen3:0.6b, POST /api/chat returned function.arguments as a JSON object. POST /v1/chat/completions, same model, same prompt, same tools array, returned the same call with function.arguments as a JSON string. Replaying either assistant message into the other endpoint was rejected with 400, each with its own parse error.

That is the whole finding, and it is a client problem rather than a server defect: each endpoint returns a well-formed call in its own encoding. The rest of this article is the measured evidence, the two error strings to grep for, a normaliser that survives both shapes, and the streaming behaviour that makes a correct client look hung.

What each specification actually says

Neither encoding is an accident. Ollama’s own API specification types tool-call arguments as an object: the ToolCall.function schema in docs.ollama.com/openapi.yaml declares

arguments:
  type: object
  description: JSON object of arguments to pass to the function

The OpenAI chat-completions schema types the same field as a string, and warns that the string is not guaranteed to be valid JSON. In the OpenAI OpenAPI specification:

arguments:
  type: string
  description: The arguments to call the function with, as generated by the model
    in JSON format.

So a client that moves between the two surfaces is not decoding the same type twice; it is decoding an object on one side and a serialised object on the other. Ollama’s OpenAI-compatibility page is explicit that the /v1 layer is partial — “Ollama supports a subset of the OpenAI API” — which is consistent with what follows. The string return on /v1 matches the OpenAI schema; the object return on /api/chat matches Ollama’s. A library that assumes one shape is correct only on the surface it was written for.

This is also the specific place where our own guide to Ollama’s two API surfaces overstates parity. Its sentence “Both approaches produce identical inference results” holds for plain text and does not hold for tool calls, as the measurement below shows. For a vanished or retyped call rather than an encoding mismatch, see the history-corruption cases; those are server-side parser and renderer defects, and they are a different failure. If you want the mechanism behind function calling first, the tool-use explainer covers it, and the tool-definition token cost piece covers what the same request spends before generation starts.

The measurement: one host, one model, one prompt

One read_file tool (path: string, max_bytes: integer, both required), one user message — “Read the file src/app.py and report the first 2000 bytes.” — sent to both endpoints of the same local server, temperature 0, native request with think: false. Environment: Ollama 0.20.3, qwen3:0.6b digest 7df6b6e09427 (Q4_K_M), 2 vCPU / 11 GB, localhost only, no credentials and no external network. Measured 2026-11-15; the two specification excerpts above were reopened on 2026-11-25 and are dated separately from the probe.

POST /api/chat POST /v1/chat/completions
HTTP status 200 200
tool-call keys id, function (index, name, arguments) id, index, type, function
function.arguments object → Python dict JSON string → Python str
argument value {"path": "src/app.py", "max_bytes": 2000} "{\"path\":\"src/app.py\",\"max_bytes\":2000}"
tool-call id call_3nn9ernp call_im2sam5h
assistant message keys role, content, tool_calls role, content, reasoning, tool_calls
stop field done_reason: "stop" finish_reason: "tool_calls"
token counts prompt_eval_count 175, eval_count 32 usage 169 / 134 / 303
wall clock (includes load) 36.9 s 74.1 s

The raw bodies are published: /api/chat request, /api/chat response, /v1 request, /v1 response.

Two details in that table matter more than they look. The native response reports done_reason: "stop" on a turn that contains a tool call, while the compatible response reports finish_reason: "tool_calls". A client that treats stop as “the model finished talking” and never inspects tool_calls will silently discard a perfectly good call on the native surface. And the /v1 message carries a reasoning field with the model’s thinking text, which the native message from this think: false request does not carry.

Wall-clock numbers are load-inclusive observations from one 2 vCPU host, not a benchmark; this article makes no throughput claim.

Two client bugs, one wire difference

The shapes fail differently in client code, which is why the same root cause produces unrelated-looking tracebacks.

Decoding an OpenAI-shaped call with json.loads works; decoding a native call that way raises TypeError: the JSON object must be str, bytes or bytearray, not dict. Consuming a native call with args["path"] works; consuming an OpenAI-shaped call that way raises TypeError: string indices must be integers, not 'str', quoted here from the interpreter rather than paraphrased — the string is indexed by "path", which Python rejects because string indices must be integers. Libraries that parse arguments in exactly one place get one of these, and libraries that parse in two places get the other on the second turn.

The history side is worse, because it is the server rejecting the request rather than the client misreading a value. Both directions were measured, and both returned 400 immediately — before generation, so 0.0 s wall:

native assistant turn -> POST /v1/chat/completions
400 {"error":{"message":"json: cannot unmarshal object into Go struct field .messages.tool_calls.function.arguments of type string","type":"invalid_request_error","param":null,"code":null}}

openai assistant turn -> POST /api/chat
400 {"error":"Value looks like object, but can't find closing '}' symbol"}

Transcripts: native history replayed into /v1 and OpenAI history replayed into /api/chat. Both files contain the exact request that was sent, so you can replay them against your own server.

Read those messages as version-scoped fingerprints rather than API contracts. The first is a Go encoding/json error naming .messages.tool_calls.function.arguments and the expected type string; the second is Ollama’s own message parser failing to read a string that looks like an object. The durable behaviour to test for is the 400 on cross-endpoint replay; the exact strings may change between releases. If a future version coerces the type instead of rejecting it, the failure disappears and this section becomes historical.

The practical consequence is a rule about what to store between turns. Keep tool calls in the encoding of the endpoint you are about to call, or keep a neutral representation and serialise at the edge. Do not pass the native assistant message straight into an OpenAI-compatible client’s history, and do not pass the OpenAI-shaped one back to /api/chat. The tool-call id is no help either. Each response generated its own call, and the two ids (call_3nn9ernp natively, call_im2sam5h on /v1) are unrelated strings, so a proxy that rewrites ids across surfaces (the layer LiteLLM-style translation deals with) still has to fix the argument type.

A normaliser that survives both shapes

The adapter below is the minimum that handles what was actually observed: object arguments, string arguments, one nested wrapper (a model occasionally emits {"arguments": "{...}"}), and the empty case where the turn carries no call at all. It validates the decoded mapping against the schema that was sent, so a string that decodes to a list or a missing required key fails loudly instead of reaching the executor.

def normalise_tool_call(message, schema):
    calls = message.get("tool_calls") or []
    if len(calls) != 1:
        raise ToolCallShapeError("expected exactly 1 tool call, found %d" % len(calls))
    fn = calls[0].get("function") or {}
    args = fn.get("arguments")
    if isinstance(args, str):
        args = json.loads(args)          # OpenAI-compatible surface
    elif isinstance(args, dict):
        args = dict(args)                # native surface
    else:
        raise ToolCallShapeError("arguments is %s" % type(args).__name__)
    if "arguments" in args and len(args) <= 2:   # model-invented wrapper
        args = json.loads(args["arguments"]) if isinstance(args["arguments"], str) else args["arguments"]
    missing = [k for k in schema.get("required", []) if k not in args]
    if missing:
        raise ToolCallShapeError("missing required argument(s): %s" % ", ".join(missing))
    return fn.get("name"), args

The listing above is a condensed variant of the published file, not a verbatim excerpt: the json import, the ToolCallShapeError class and the per-property type checks are omitted for space, and the full file is normalise_tool_call.py, with per-property type validation. Its --selftest runs four cases — the two measured shapes plus the nested wrapper and the empty turn — using the exact argument objects returned by this run. Those four checks passed on Python 3.12.3 at 2026-11-25T12:54:29Z; the captured run is normalise_selftest_output.txt. That is a local fixture check of the adapter, not a model measurement: no model was called to produce it.

Streaming: 2 chunks versus 100, and why a correct client looks hung

Streaming was measured on the same prompt. The native surface produced 2 NDJSON chunks in 5.1 s, with the complete call inside the message object of the first chunk: tool_calls_per_chunk was [1, 0], no content and no thinking text.

The OpenAI-compatible surface produced 100 SSE chunks in 42.9 s. Of those, 98 carried delta.reasoning (394 characters in total), none carried delta.content, and exactly one carried the tool call — whole, with the arguments string not fragmented across deltas. The run’s usage block was absent from the stream. Raw chunk dumps: native and /v1.

A client written against the native stream expects the first chunk to be the answer. On the compatible stream it receives dozens of chunks whose content is empty and whose only payload is reasoning text, so its idle timer, its “first token” log line and its progress bar all behave as though the server were stuck — while the server is generating normally. The extra time is a property of this probe’s request rather than a claim about the endpoint: the native call here carried think: false, while the /v1/chat/completions request carried no thinking control at all and still came back with 394 reasoning characters in the stream and a reasoning field in the non-streamed message, which is why the same call took 42.9 s streamed and 74.1 s non-streamed against 5.1 s and 36.9 s natively. Ollama’s compatibility page documents reasoning_effort and reasoning.effort as thinking control on that surface, with "none" requesting false for boolean-only models; this run sent neither field, so it tested neither and says nothing about whether they would suppress the reasoning text on 0.20.3.

Two cautions before copying the usual SSE advice. First, this run did not observe fragmented arguments: the whole call arrived in one delta, so the article does not claim fragmentation happens on this model. A robust client should still assemble fragments, because that is the documented OpenAI behaviour, but this measurement is not evidence that it occurs here. Second, chunk counts, reasoning volume and wall times are this run’s observations, not constants; only the argument type, the status codes and the error bodies were stable enough to treat as findings.

What this is not

  • Not an Ollama bug. Both endpoints returned a correct, self-consistent call, and the compatibility layer is documented as a subset. The mismatch lives in clients that assume one encoding.
  • Not a statement about hosted OpenAI. No request was sent to api.openai.com; the OpenAI schema is cited only because the /v1 layer imitates it.
  • Not generalisable beyond this setup. One version (0.20.3), one model (qwen3:0.6b, digest 7df6b6e09427), one prompt, one host. Another model may serialise differently or emit no call at all.
  • Not a performance result. Wall-clock times include model load and are reported as observations from a 2 vCPU machine.

Reproduce it against your own server

Everything needed to re-run the probe and diff your server version is published with this page. shape_probe.py is standard-library Python: it posts to /api/chat with think: false, posts the same messages and tools to /v1/chat/completions, streams both, replays each assistant turn into the opposite endpoint, and writes one JSON file per step. METHOD.md records the environment and the determinism caveats, and 00_summary.json is the machine-readable summary behind every table cell above.

Run it as python3 shape_probe.py <out_dir> against a local Ollama with qwen3:0.6b pulled. It contacts localhost only — no credentials, no paid API, no external network — and takes roughly two to three minutes on 2 vCPU, most of it in the /v1 reasoning tokens. If your run returns string arguments on both endpoints, or accepts cross-endpoint replay, that is a real result too: name your version and model, because the behaviour is version-scoped and your negative result supersedes this one for your deployment.

The fix in your own code is small and does not need a server change: normalise the arguments at the boundary, keep history in the encoding of the endpoint you will call next, and do not read done_reason: "stop" as proof that nothing was called.

item.title: vLLM Tool-Call Streaming: Detecting Corrupted Arguments
item.description: Three vLLM reports filed in October 2026 show merged, truncated and dropped tool-call arguments at different version scopes. Here is how to localize the fault and gate execution.
item.content:encoded:
A streaming tool call can reach your agent corrupted while every SSE frame on the wire is valid JSON. The damage shows up after reassembly: two calls fused into one, an argument string cut mid-token, or a number that became the string "3". The request returns HTTP 200, finish_reason says tool_calls, and an agent that trusts the payload executes the wrong thing. The practical question is not whether vLLM is “broken” in general; it is whether the corruption is in the server’s parser or in your client’s reassembly, and how to stop execution until that is settled. This article separates what the current primary reports actually establish, shows how to localize the fault with a raw SSE capture, and ships a small gate that refuses any call whose arguments do not round-trip against your declared schema.

What the three October 2026 reports actually establish

The first report is vllm-project/vllm#64012, filed 2026-10-27 and still open. It is explicitly a legacy-version report: the reporter confirms the failure on vLLM 0.19.0 with vllm/tool_parsers/qwen3xml_tool_parser.py at SHA256 7c2ba229b0b6dcd061b9f581390a5fb892a2fc20023b20656d91706522f311bd, states that the v0.19.1 source is byte-identical, and says the reproduction needs no GPU, weights, tokenizer or network. Two independent <tool_call> blocks parse correctly when they arrive in one chunk or when the split falls between the calls. When a chunk holds the first call’s closing tags plus the opening of the second, the same concatenated text produces malformed JSON and can truncate a string value. The reporter adds that #45003 removed the old XML parser and #45413 introduced newer engine routing, and calls this “the legacy v0.19.0 implementation, not an asserted regression on current main.” That boundary matters: reading this thread as evidence about v0.32.x is a version error.

The second report, vllm-project/vllm#63983, is a different failure and a different scope. It was filed 2026-10-27 and closed as completed on 2026-11-02 with no closing comment, so read the report as evidence of what the parser did, not as an open ticket. Against main at commit 5d35ce3, with parser code only and no GPU, the functiongemma parser extracts arguments written as key:<escape>value<escape>. FunctionGemma’s own chat template wraps only strings that way; numbers, booleans, arrays and objects are emitted bare, never match the parser’s regex, and are silently dropped. The issue’s printed output makes the consequence concrete: a set_alarm call carrying hour:7, enabled:true, days:[mon,tue] and snooze:{minutes:5} comes back as {"label": "Wake up"}. The call “succeeds” with four of its five arguments missing.

The third, vllm-project/vllm#63941, concerns Kimi K3 at main commit cd9aa5b5ee (2026-10-26), also parser-level and CPU-only. When a generation is cut inside an XTML control marker by max_tokens, the non-streaming path returns the raw partial marker text as user-visible content, while the streaming path withholds the same fragment. The two paths disagree about the same tokens. The reporter notes that current main tip 6fe3d447ac does not touch kimi_k3_tool_parser.py.

Report Version scope Symptom What the report does not show
#64012 v0.19.0 legacy qwen3_xml Merged/truncated arguments when a chunk straddles two calls Any regression on current releases; v0.19.1 was never executed
#63983 main @ 5d35ce3, functiongemma Non-string arguments silently dropped Chunk-boundary behaviour; other parser families
#63941 main @ cd9aa5b5ee, Kimi K3 Non-streaming leaks a partial XTML marker that streaming withholds That the leak affects schema-valid calls or other parsers

Read together, the three reports support a failure class, not one release-wide defect: chunk-boundary merge and truncation in a legacy parser, silent argument loss in one current parser, and stream/non-stream divergence in another. No single tag is shown to carry all three symptoms, and none of the reports is a measurement of your deployment. The adjacent Ubicloud write-up is often cited alongside them and should not be: it measured schema accuracy, not chunk boundaries. It reports 92% schema accuracy serving Kimi K2.6 on vLLM 0.28 against the 2,000-request K2VV ToolCall workload, 100% after constrained decoding was enabled as a vLLM 0.31 server flag, and a drop to 91% when a later release changed the default. That is a constrained-decoding story about argument validity, and it is useful context for why strictness flags exist. It is not evidence that streaming splits corrupt calls.

The flag semantics that matter, pinned to v0.32.0

The current stable release on 2026-10-28 is v0.32.0 (published 2026-10-18), followed by v0.31.0 and v0.30.0, according to the release list. The tool-calling documentation pinned to that tag defines the startup flags plainly: --enable-auto-tool-choice is mandatory for automatic tool choice, --tool-call-parser selects the parser, --tool-parser-plugin optionally registers a custom one, and --chat-template is optional. It also states the division of labour that this article is about: “Remember that it’s the caller’s responsibility to … Handle the tool calls in your application logic.” The server flags choose and drive a parser; they do not certify the arguments your application is about to execute.

The same page documents the strictness behaviour that changed the risk picture in this release line. Structural tags constrain the tool-call envelope (markup and function name) always for tool_choice="required" and named calls, and for tool_choice="auto" only once a tool sets strict: true or the server raises the floor. Argument schemas are pinned only for tools marked strict: true, or under --tool-strict-level parameter. The --tool-strict-level values are auto (default, follow the request), function (constrain envelope for every request with tools), and parameter (pin every tool’s argument schema). VLLM_ENFORCE_STRICT_TOOL_CALLING defaults to true and, when false, disables structural tags entirely. The page names the reason a gate is still needed: with tool_choice="auto" and no strict tools, “the model generates tool calls without any grammar and malformed markup can leak into the response.”

Parser coverage is version-specific too. The v0.32.0 page lists FunctionGemma under functiongemma and Kimi-K2 under kimi_k2; the string kimi_k3 does not appear on that page at all. So the Kimi K3 defect in #63941 is a main-branch parser report, not a documented v0.32.0 parser you can select by reading this page.

Localize the fault before you patch anything

Three checks separate a server parser defect from a client reassembly defect, and they take minutes rather than a GPU rental.

First, capture the stream verbatim. curl -N --no-buffer with your normal request body, redirected to a file, preserves event framing, data: lines and chunk order. Second, replay that capture through the exact buffering code your agent uses, splitting the captured bytes at every offset. A client that decodes each TCP read independently will fail inside multi-byte characters; a client that trims whitespace or re-serialises arguments will fail on types. Third, send the same prompt non-streaming and compare the resulting calls. If the raw deltas concatenate to valid JSON and the non-streaming call matches, the fault is client-side reassembly. If the raw deltas themselves are invalid or short, the fault is upstream of your client. If both parse but disagree on types or call count, suspect the parser or the model’s chat template rather than transport.

The gate published with this article includes that boundary replay as a selftest. It builds a five-event stream carrying two parallel calls, serialises it as OpenAI SSE frames, and re-runs reassembly plus validation at all 760 byte offsets. All 760 splits reassembled without a false rejection, which is the property you want before you trust a gate to tell you that a real corruption is real. That number comes from the run record in this article’s evidence directory; it is a fixture check, not a vLLM measurement.

A gate that runs before dispatch

The gate is deliberately boring: reassemble the stream the way the OpenAI-compatible client does, parse each arguments string as JSON, then compare the parsed object with the schema the model was given. It fails closed on five conditions - unparseable JSON, non-object arguments, missing required fields, a JSON type that does not match the declaration, and a call count that differs from what the request expected. Types are compared exactly, because Python’s bool is a subclass of int and because accepting "3" where integer was declared is precisely the silent retyping a coercing client can produce.

def validate(calls, tools, expected_calls):
    issues = []
    if expected_calls is not None and len(calls) != expected_calls:
        issues.append(("CALL_COUNT_MISMATCH", f"{len(calls)} of {expected_calls}"))
    for call in calls:
        spec = tools.get(call["name"])
        try:
            args = json.loads(call["arguments"])
        except ValueError:
            issues.append(("ARGUMENTS_NOT_JSON", call["name"])); continue
        for name in spec.get("required", []):
            if name not in args:
                issues.append(("MISSING_REQUIRED", name))
        for name, value in args.items():
            declared = spec["properties"].get(name, {}).get("type")
            if declared and type_name(value) not in declared:
                issues.append(("TYPE_MISMATCH", f"{name}={value!r}"))
    return issues

Call it on the assembled message, before any tool dispatcher or agent loop sees it. On a rejection, log the raw arguments string and the finish_reason, return the errors to the model as a tool result if your loop supports that, and retry. Do not coerce values to make the call pass: coercion converts a detected type error into an undetected wrong argument, which is the failure this gate exists to prevent.

The published selftest exercises four constructed corruptions derived from the clean fixture, and each is caught by a distinct code rather than by a generic exception:

Constructed corruption Detected as Calls reassembled
Two calls merged into one delta ARGUMENTS_NOT_JSON + CALL_COUNT_MISMATCH 1 of 2
Arguments cut mid-string ARGUMENTS_NOT_JSON 2
Integer, boolean, array re-encoded as strings TYPE_MISMATCH 2
Non-string arguments dropped MISSING_REQUIRED 2

Two limits follow from the design. A merged call cannot be reconstructed, only rejected, so the correct recovery is a retry with the error surfaced, not a repair heuristic. And a schema-valid but semantically wrong argument - the failure class Ubicloud measured - passes the gate by definition; strict decoding and a stronger schema are the tools for that, not this check.

What is verified, what is not

Everything about the three reports above was re-read from the GitHub API on 2026-10-28 between 12:01:39 and 12:01:43 UTC, the window recorded in the research fetch log for this article, and the pinned documentation and release list were fetched inside that same window. The gate and its fixtures were executed in the same session, and the run record captures the command, exit code, stdout and input hashes. What was not done matters just as much: vLLM is not installed in this workspace image, so no parser was imported and no claim is made that any listed defect reproduces at v0.32.0. The reports’ own commits and version labels are quoted as the reporters stated them. There is no throughput, latency, cost or accuracy measurement here, and no claim that all vLLM parsers are affected - the matrix is one legacy parser, one current parser family and one current stream/non-stream divergence.

If you operate a vLLM endpoint for an agent, the operational order is: pin the tag you actually run, capture one streaming and one non-streaming response with parallel calls, replay the capture at every byte boundary through your client, and enable the gate before the next deploy. If the corruption survives that sequence at a pinned tag, you have a reproducible parser report to file rather than an intermittent symptom to describe.

Sources

Primary sources, all re-fetched on 2026-10-28 UTC:

  • #64012, legacy qwen3_xml chunk-boundary report - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/64012
  • #63983, FunctionGemma non-string argument drop - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/63983
  • #63941, Kimi K3 stream/non-stream marker leak - https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/63941
  • Published releases and dates (v0.32.0 latest stable in this window) - https://api.github.com/repos/vllm-project/vllm/releases?per_page=6
  • Tool-calling flags, strict mode and --tool-strict-level, pinned to v0.32.0 - https://docs.vllm.ai/en/v0.32.0/features/tool_calling.html
  • Adjacent schema-accuracy measurement (different failure class; not chunk boundaries) - https://www.ubicloud.com/blog/fixing-tool-call-accuracy-in-vllm

First-party artifacts published with this article (constructed fixtures, no model output; local fixture check, not vendor measurement):

  • Gate and boundary selftest - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/toolcall_gate.py
  • Parallel-call SSE fixture - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/fixtures/sse_parallel_toolcalls.json
  • Declared tool schema used by the gate - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/fixtures/tool_schema.json
  • Run record: command, exit code, stdout, input hashes - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/baeseokjae/baeseokjae.github.io/main/research/evidence/vllm-streaming-tool-call-parser-corruption-2026/first-party-fixture-run-2026-10-28.json

For the argument shapes a parser is supposed to produce, see LLM function calling and tool use; for why this serving stack was chosen before parsing became the concern, see vLLM vs Ollama in production and local model serving frameworks compared.
